details:
IKIRERE-X: Astronaut Health Intelligence

Team: INGABO X
Location: Kigali, Rwanda
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
OUR CHALLENGE: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions

Project Overview

IKIRERE-X is a web-based astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed to help astronauts and authorized medical support teams observe, record, and review important health indicators during space missions.

Space exploration exposes astronauts to demanding conditions, including microgravity, isolation, confinement, changes in sleep patterns, and distance from Earth-based medical support. These conditions make continuous health awareness and effective communication important for crew safety and mission success.

Our project provides a centralized digital dashboard that organizes health measurements and wellness information into an understandable format. Its goal is to help identify unusual changes, make health information easier to review, and support informed follow-up.

What Does IKIRERE-X Do?

The software provides several main functions:

  • Vital-sign monitoring: Displays heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, and blood pressure.
  • Crew profiles: Allows users to switch between illustrative crew profiles.
  • Health history: Records measurements and displays recent entries.
  • Trend awareness: Helps users observe changes in measurements over time.
  • Informational alerts: Highlights readings that cross configured demonstration thresholds.
  • Wellness monitoring: Records sleep duration, stress levels, physical activity, and reported symptoms.
  • Health reports: Provides CSV export and a printable report to support information sharing and review.

The current prototype uses simulated astronaut readings and manually entered measurements. It does not yet connect to real astronaut monitoring equipment or live NASA telemetry.

How Does It Work?

IKIRERE-X follows a simple five-step process:

Step 1 – Capture: A user selects a crew profile and enters a health measurement or wellness observation.

Step 2 – Organize: The application records the information and displays it in the selected crew member's dashboard.

Step 3 – Compare: Users review current readings alongside previous measurements to understand changes over time.

Step 4 – Alert: The system displays an informational warning when a configured demonstration threshold is crossed.

Step 5 – Review and report: Users examine the information and can export a CSV file or generate a printable report for further review.

These alerts are not medical diagnoses or emergency instructions. Any operational thresholds would need validation by qualified medical professionals and alignment with approved mission procedures.

Benefits and Intended Impact

IKIRERE-X aims to provide the following benefits:

  • Makes important health information easier to understand in one dashboard.
  • Helps users recognize changes in health measurements and wellness patterns.
  • Organizes health observations into a structured history.
  • Supports communication through downloadable reports.
  • Provides a foundation for future integration with wearable health-monitoring devices.
  • Encourages proactive health awareness during long-duration missions.

The intended long-term impact is to support safer human space exploration by making astronaut health information more accessible and easier to review. With further development and validation, similar monitoring approaches could also be explored for remote research stations, isolated environments, and other settings where access to medical support is limited.

NASA Data and Scientific Foundation

NASA human-spaceflight research informs the problem addressed by IKIRERE-X. NASA's Human Research Program identifies important risks associated with spaceflight, including physiological changes, behavioral health challenges, and other hazards.

We consulted NASA resources, including:

  • NASA Human Research Program – Risks of Human Spaceflight.
  • NASA-STD-3001 Volume 1 – Crew Health.
  • NASA Crew Health Records guidance.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository as a potential source for future research-data integration.

These resources help inform the project's purpose and design. The current software demonstration uses simulated measurements; it does not claim to have integrated raw NASA research datasets or live astronaut health records.

Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies

We developed IKIRERE-X as a lightweight web application using:

HTML5: Creates the website structure, dashboard sections, measurement forms, crew profiles, and tables.

CSS3: Provides the visual design, dark space-inspired interface, responsive layout, cards, and navigation.

JavaScript: Powers user interactions, measurement entry, simulated crew data, informational alerts, wellness logging, and report exports.

Browser localStorage: Stores prototype entries locally in the user's browser. It does not provide cloud synchronization or centralized medical-record storage.

Python and python-pptx: Used to programmatically prepare and format the project's PowerPoint presentation.

InfinityFree: Selected as a potential free hosting platform for making the website publicly accessible.

No physical medical sensors, wearable devices, or external hardware are currently connected to the prototype.

What Makes IKIRERE-X Creative?

The project's creativity comes from combining several health-monitoring functions in one astronaut-focused interface.

Instead of displaying isolated measurements alone, IKIRERE-X brings together vital signs, personal measurement history, wellness observations, informational alerts, and report generation.

Its individual crew profiles support a future approach based on personal health baselines, where changes can be considered in relation to an astronaut's own history rather than relying only on generic values.

The interface is also designed to be understandable and extendable. Its lightweight web architecture provides a foundation for future integrations with secure databases, wearable devices, and validated research-data sources.

8. Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors:

Astronaut safety: Health information must be presented responsibly. The prototype does not diagnose conditions or replace medical professionals.

Usability: The dashboard should make information understandable without requiring complicated navigation.

Accessibility: A web-based interface makes the prototype easier to access across supported devices.

Data privacy: Health information is sensitive. The current local-storage prototype is not designed for operational medical records. Future versions will require secure authentication, encryption, access controls, and appropriate data-protection procedures.

Scientific validity: Monitoring thresholds and interpretation methods must be supported by appropriate scientific evidence and validated before real-world medical or spaceflight use.

Scalability: The software structure should allow future development of wearable-device connections, secure data synchronization, and research-data integration.

Cost and sustainability: We selected standard web technologies to make the initial prototype affordable to develop, test, and demonstrate.

Future Development

Our next development stages include:

  1. Integrating validated wearable sensors for automated health measurements.
  2. Connecting a secure backend for authorized data synchronization.
  3. Studying relevant NASA Open Science Data Repository datasets and integrating suitable research data with clear attribution.
  4. Developing stronger trend-analysis and personalized baseline features.
  5. Working with qualified medical and human-factors experts to validate alert logic and usability.
  6. Improving cybersecurity, privacy, reliability, and mission-specific access controls.
  7. Evaluating the software through controlled research or pilot programmes.

Conclusion

IKIRERE-X is built around a simple but important idea: astronaut health information should be organized, understandable, and available for informed review.

By combining vital-sign recording, wellness observations, trend awareness, informational alerts, and reporting in one web-based prototype, INGABO X is exploring a practical digital approach to astronaut health monitoring.

Our vision is to develop IKIRERE-X into a secure, scientifically validated, and extensible platform that can contribute to healthier crews and safer future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

IKIRERE-X – Protecting life. Supporting the next frontier.
